title: Hannover Re 9M Profit Rises 6.9% to EUR 2.1B, Target Confirmed
summary: Hannover Re reported nine-month 2026 net income of EUR 2.1 billion, up 6.9%, with a third-quarter profit of EUR 695 million, a property and casualty combined ratio of 83.7% and a Solvency II ratio of 242%, and it confirmed its target of at least EUR 2.7 billion for the year.
description:
Hannover Re, the German reinsurance group, reported a strong first nine months of 2026 on November 9. Group net income reached EUR 2.1 billion, up 6.9% from the same period of 2025, and the company said it is on course to meet its full-year target of at least EUR 2.7 billion. This article sets out the numbers from the company's results as reported by the Boersen-Zeitung and Insurance Edge, explains what the main measures mean, and notes what the figures do not show. It is a summary of public information and is not investment advice.

The headline numbers

For the nine months to September 30, 2026, Hannover Re reported group net income of EUR 2.1 billion, compared with about EUR 2.0 billion a year earlier, a rise of 6.9%. Earnings per share were EUR 17.42, against EUR 16.29. In the third quarter alone, net income was EUR 695 million, against EUR 651 million in the third quarter of 2025, and the Boersen-Zeitung said that figure beat market expectations by 9%.

Gross reinsurance revenue was EUR 19.5 billion, slightly below the EUR 19.7 billion of the prior period in reported terms, though up 1.1% at unchanged exchange rates. The reinsurance service result, which is the underwriting profit measure under the IFRS 17 accounting standard, rose to EUR 2.6 billion from EUR 2.4 billion. Operating profit, known as EBIT, climbed 16.5% to EUR 2.9 billion from EUR 2.5 billion. Return on equity was 21.1%, a little lower than the 22.0% of a year earlier, because shareholders' equity grew to EUR 13.7 billion from EUR 12.9 billion at the end of 2025.

Property and casualty reinsurance

The property and casualty business is Hannover Re's largest. Its gross revenue fell 4.9% to EUR 13.2 billion, but its net reinsurance service result rose to EUR 1.9 billion from EUR 1.7 billion, and operating profit increased 20.2% to EUR 2.2 billion. The combined ratio, which compares claims and costs with premium so that anything below 100% is an underwriting profit, was 83.7%, an improvement from 86.0%. The company had told investors it expected a ratio below 87% for the full year, so the nine-month figure sits comfortably inside that guide.

The main reason is the level of large losses. Hannover Re paid EUR 1,316 million of large losses, which covers natural catastrophes and other major claims, compared with EUR 1,177 million in the prior period. That is higher than a year ago in absolute terms, but it is about EUR 470 million below the pro-rata budget of EUR 1,786.5 million for the nine months. The full-year large loss budget is EUR 2.3 billion. The Boersen-Zeitung reported that Hannover Re may add some of the unused budget to its balance sheet if losses stay well below the budget through the year end, a practice that builds a buffer for later years.

One figure points the other way. New business contractual service margin in property and casualty, a measure of profit expected to be earned from new contracts, fell 11.9% to EUR 2.3 billion from EUR 2.6 billion. That is consistent with lower revenue and with the remarks from management about competition, discussed below.

Life and health reinsurance

Life and health reinsurance grew faster in revenue terms. Gross revenue rose 9.5% at constant exchange rates to EUR 6.3 billion, against EUR 5.8 billion. The net reinsurance service result was EUR 717.2 million, compared with EUR 671.3 million, and the company has a full-year target for this segment of around EUR 925 million. Operating profit was EUR 668.2 million, up 3.5% from EUR 645.3 million. New contractual service margin generation was EUR 502.8 million, lower than the EUR 584.8 million of the prior period.

Investments and capital

Hannover Re's investment result for the nine months was EUR 1.9 billion, up 40.4%, according to the Boersen-Zeitung. The annualised investment return at the end of September was 3.7%, above the company's target of about 3.5%. The Solvency II ratio, the European measure of how much capital an insurer holds compared with what regulators require, was 242% at September 30, compared with 256% at the end of 2025 and a target of more than 200%. A ratio above 200% is generally viewed as a strong capital position, although the fall of 14 points over nine months shows that growth, dividends and market movements all use up capital.

Guidance and what comes next

Hannover Re confirmed that it expects group net income of at least EUR 2.7 billion in 2026, up from the EUR 2.6 billion it had guided for 2025. With EUR 2.1 billion already booked after nine months, the company would need roughly EUR 600 million in the fourth quarter to reach the minimum, which is below the third-quarter result of EUR 695 million. That arithmetic is ours, and the fourth quarter depends on large losses and on market returns. Guidance for 2027 will be given at an investor day on November 25.

Chief executive Clemens Jungsthoefel said the company was thoroughly satisfied with the first nine months and very confident of reaching its full-year guidance. Chief financial officer Christian Hermelingmeier told the Boersen-Zeitung that the company is very much on track, that reinsurance prices remain at a good level, and that he expects the rise in competition to continue for now.

How to read the competition comment

Reinsurance pricing moves in cycles. After several years of strong pricing, more capital has entered the market, and when supply grows, reinsurers have to accept lower prices or less favorable terms to keep business. The reported decline in property and casualty revenue and in new business margin is consistent with that picture, although the sources do not say how much of the revenue decline comes from price and how much from currency effects or from deliberate choices to write less. Readers should treat the comment as a signal of direction, not a forecast. Reinsurance contracts are renewed on set dates, with many property catastrophe programs renewing on January 1, and the pricing outcome of those renewals will be visible in company statements early next year.

What it means for readers

Most people never buy reinsurance, but it affects them. When reinsurers are profitable and well capitalised, they are willing to keep selling protection to the insurers that cover homes and cars, and that supports availability of cover after large disasters. When reinsurance prices fall, primary insurers may see lower costs, although whether that reaches customers depends on competition in each market. Investors who follow the sector can watch the combined ratio, the pace of large losses against budget and the solvency ratio.

What the report does not show

The sources reviewed here do not give a breakdown of the third-quarter combined ratio or of third-quarter large losses, and the Boersen-Zeitung article did not report EBIT or the combined ratio, which came from the Insurance Edge summary of the company's release. Readers who want the full detail can read the company's quarterly statement, published on its investor relations site. This article summarises public reporting and is not financial advice.
source_name: Hannover Re (nine-month 2026 results, November 9, 2026) as reported by Boersen-Zeitung and Insurance Edge

key_points: Hannover Re's group net income for the first nine months of 2026 was EUR 2.1 billion, up 6.9% from about EUR 2.0 billion a year earlier, and third-quarter net income was EUR 695 million against EUR 651 million.

The property and casualty reinsurance combined ratio improved to 83.7% from 86.0%, better than the company's full-year expectation of below 87%, helped by large losses of EUR 1,316 million that stayed well under the nine-month budget of EUR 1,786.5 million.
Group operating profit (EBIT) rose 16.5% to EUR 2.9 billion and earnings per share reached EUR 17.42, while return on equity eased to 21.1% from 22.0%.

why_it_matters: Reinsurers absorb the biggest insurance losses so that primary insurers can keep writing cover for homes, cars and businesses. Hannover Re's results show how profitable that job has been in a year of lighter large losses, and its comments about competition hint at how the price of reinsurance may behave as primary insurers renew their programs.

title: Munich Re Q3 Net Result EUR 1.74B as Earthquake Lifts Major Losses
summary: Munich Re's final third-quarter 2026 statement shows a net result of EUR 1.742 billion, down from EUR 1.997 billion, as major losses of EUR 646 million, including EUR 300 million from a Colombian earthquake, lifted its reinsurance combined ratio to 80%, while nine-month profit rose to EUR 5.667 billion and the 2026 target stayed at EUR 6.6 billion.
description:
Munich Re published its full third-quarter 2026 statement on November 12, filling in the detail behind the preliminary figures it released on October 23. The German reinsurer earned EUR 1.742 billion in the quarter, lower than a year earlier, but its nine-month result climbed to EUR 5.667 billion, and it kept the full-year target of EUR 6.6 billion that it had raised in October. This article summarises the numbers as reported by Artemis and Reinsurance News from the company's statement, explains the main terms, and notes what is not yet known. It is a summary of public information and is not investment advice.

The group result

Munich Re's net result for the third quarter was EUR 1.742 billion, compared with EUR 1.997 billion in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months, the result was EUR 5.667 billion, up from EUR 5.176 billion. The preliminary figure in October was approximately EUR 1.7 billion, so the final statement confirms it. Group insurance revenue in the quarter was EUR 16.626 billion, up from EUR 14.575 billion, and for nine months it was EUR 46.583 billion, up from EUR 45.162 billion.

The quarter's total technical result, which measures underwriting profit under IFRS 17, was EUR 2.375 billion, down from EUR 2.822 billion. The operating result was EUR 2.472 billion, against EUR 3.036 billion. Annualised return on equity was 20.2% for the quarter, compared with 24.2% a year earlier, and 21.9% for nine months, compared with 20.8%. The investment result for the quarter was EUR 1.859 billion, against EUR 2.385 billion, a return of 3.2% on average market value.

Property and casualty reinsurance

The largest segment, property and casualty reinsurance, earned EUR 938 million in the quarter, down from EUR 1.187 billion. Its combined ratio, the share of premium that goes to claims and costs, was 80%, compared with 62.7% in the third quarter of 2025. A combined ratio of 80% still means a healthy underwriting profit, but the move from the very low level of the previous year reflects higher major losses. Insurance revenue in the segment was EUR 4.446 billion, up from EUR 4.241 billion. Over nine months, gross revenue was EUR 12.4 billion, down 9%, which Munich Re attributes to currency and renewal effects.

Major losses, meaning large individual claims and catastrophe events counted after retrocession, which is the reinsurance that reinsurers buy for themselves, and before tax, were EUR 646 million in the quarter, compared with EUR 118 million a year earlier. Natural disasters accounted for EUR 514 million of that, and the Colombian El Choco earthquake was the costliest event at EUR 300 million. The company said major losses were 14.9% of net insurance revenue. That is far above last year's 2.9% but below the 18% that Munich Re expects over a full year, so the quarter was still lighter than its planning assumption.

ERGO and other segments

ERGO, the group's primary insurance and health business, earned EUR 263 million in the quarter, compared with EUR 304 million, and EUR 819 million over nine months, compared with EUR 796 million. ERGO's insurance revenue rose to EUR 6.192 billion in the quarter from EUR 5.313 billion, and to EUR 17.36 billion over nine months from EUR 16.019 billion.

Life and health reinsurance improved. Its quarterly net result rose to EUR 340 million from EUR 286 million, and its total technical result to EUR 493 million from EUR 314 million. Global Specialty Insurance earned EUR 201 million, compared with EUR 221 million, with a combined ratio of 83.9% against 82.8%. The whole reinsurance segment, which combines property and casualty with life and health, earned EUR 1.479 billion in the quarter, against EUR 1.693 billion, and EUR 4.849 billion over nine months, against EUR 4.380 billion.

Guidance

In October, when Munich Re released preliminary figures, it raised its net result target for 2026 by EUR 300 million, from EUR 6.3 billion to EUR 6.6 billion, and it kept that figure in the full statement. It also said it expects a net combined ratio in property and casualty reinsurance of below 80% for the year and a ratio below 90% for Global Specialty Insurance. The company noted in October that it may strengthen its balance sheet in the fourth quarter, depending on how major losses develop. Nine months of profit stand at EUR 5.667 billion, so the full-year target implies roughly EUR 0.9 billion in the final quarter, a simple calculation that depends on large losses and market returns.

Chief financial officer Andrew Buchanan said Munich Re achieved profitable growth in the first nine months and that the higher profit target reflects very pleasing operating performance across all business segments.

Why the combined ratio jump is not alarming

A move from 62.7% to 80% sounds large. The earlier figure was unusually low because major losses were only EUR 118 million, a very quiet quarter. An 80% ratio is in line with what the company is guiding for the year, and the major loss ratio of 14.9% was below the 18% it budgets. In plain terms, the third quarter of 2025 was unusually benign and the third quarter of 2026 was closer to normal, with one costly earthquake. Investors and analysts usually look at several quarters together for this reason, since catastrophe losses are lumpy.

What it means for readers

Reinsurance is the layer of protection behind home, car and business insurance. When a large event such as an earthquake hits, reinsurers pay part of the bill, and strong results mean they keep the capacity to do so. For ordinary policyholders the link is indirect. Price changes at the January renewals of reinsurance contracts can eventually influence what primary insurers charge, but each market also depends on local competition and claims. The sources reviewed here do not report reinsurance price changes, so this article makes no prediction.

What to watch next

Watch Munich Re's results for the full year, the pricing and terms of the January 2027 renewals, and the way major losses develop in the fourth quarter, including hurricane or wildfire events. The company publishes its quarterly statements and presentations on its investor relations website. This article summarises public reporting and is not financial advice.

key_points: Munich Re's group net result for the third quarter of 2026 was EUR 1.742 billion, against EUR 1.997 billion a year earlier, and the nine-month result rose to EUR 5.667 billion from EUR 5.176 billion.

Property and casualty reinsurance earned EUR 938 million in the quarter, down from EUR 1.187 billion, and its combined ratio was 80% against 62.7% a year earlier, because major losses rose to EUR 646 million from EUR 118 million.

Natural disasters cost EUR 514 million in the quarter, and the Colombian El Choco earthquake was the costliest single event at EUR 300 million, while major losses still came to 14.9% of net insurance revenue, below the 18% the company expected.
ERGO, the primary insurance arm, earned EUR 263 million in the quarter and EUR 819 million over nine months, and life and health reinsurance rose to EUR 340 million from EUR 286 million.
The full-year net result target stays at EUR 6.6 billion, raised by EUR 300 million from EUR 6.3 billion in October, with a property and casualty reinsurance combined ratio guided to below 80%.
why_it_matters: Munich Re is one of the largest reinsurers, the companies that insure the insurers. A quarter in which a single earthquake and other disasters push claims higher, yet profit stays above EUR 1.7 billion, shows how much cushion the industry built in a period of strong pricing, and it helps explain why reinsurers are still comfortable with their full-year profit targets.

title: Intact Q3 Operating EPS Falls 19% as Storms Lift Combined Ratio
summary: Intact Financial's third-quarter 2026 net operating income per share fell 19% to C$3.63 and net income dropped to C$562 million as about C$660 million of catastrophe losses, mostly on Canadian home insurance, lifted the combined ratio to 94.0%, even though premiums grew 5% to C$7.0 billion and operating return on equity stayed at 16%.
description:
Intact Financial Corporation, the largest property and casualty insurer in Canada, reported its third-quarter 2026 results on November 4. Storms, floods and wildfires pulled profit down sharply from a year earlier, yet premiums still grew and the company kept a double-digit return on equity. This article summarises the figures as reported by Insurance Business, explains the main terms, and notes what the report does not say. It is a summary of public information, not financial advice, and all amounts are in Canadian dollars unless stated.

The headline numbers

Net operating income per share, the measure management uses to track underlying earnings, fell 19% to C$3.63 from C$4.46 a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share fell 36% to C$3.03, and net income attributable to common shareholders was C$562 million, compared with C$861 million. Operating direct premiums written, the amount of premium the insurer sold before reinsurance, rose 5% to C$7.006 billion, led by personal lines such as home and auto.

Underwriting income, which is the profit left after claims and the costs of writing business, fell 38% to C$368 million. The group combined ratio rose to 94.0% from 89.8%. A combined ratio under 100% means premiums covered claims and expenses, so Intact still made an underwriting profit, but the margin was narrower. Other income lines were healthier: distribution income, from the brokerage businesses Intact owns, rose 16% to C$171 million, and operating net investment income rose 5% to C$422 million.

The catastrophe bill

The main driver was weather. Catastrophe losses for the quarter were about C$660 million before tax, net of reinsurance, and the company said they ran about four points above what it expected for the quarter. In Canada, flooding, wind damage and wildfires in British Columbia produced C$615 million of pre-tax catastrophe losses, net of reinsurance.

Personal property insurance took the largest share, with C$390 million of catastrophe losses. Those losses added 33 points to the Canadian personal property combined ratio, which came in at 105.0%, so that line lost money on an underwriting basis in the quarter. Commercial lines had C$173 million of catastrophe losses, and personal auto had C$52 million. The pattern is typical of summer storms: hail, flood and wind hit roofs, basements and buildings far more than cars on the road, although hail can also damage vehicles.

Over the last twelve months, catastrophe losses have totalled C$1.29 billion, modestly above the C$1.20 billion that Intact guides for a year. Chief financial officer Ken Anderson is cited on the trailing figure in the report, which signals that management is watching the annual total, not just the quarter.

Growth by region

Premium growth was solid in Canada, where operating direct premiums written rose 7% to C$4.939 billion. In the UK and Ireland, premiums were flat at C$1.078 billion, and in the United States they rose 3% to C$989 million. The US business reported a combined ratio of 85.2%, and Insurance Business said strong new business came from its most profitable US lines. The article did not report a Canada-wide combined ratio or any UK figures beyond premiums, so a full regional picture needs the company's own release.

Capital and returns

Book value per share rose 8% to C$111.11. Intact's operating return on equity, a measure of how much profit it earns on shareholders' capital, was 16%, and chief executive Charles Brindamour pointed to that figure as a sign of the resilience of the platform. Over the last twelve months, the company bought back C$581 million of shares, and its total capital margin, the cushion of capital above the level it needs, was C$3.6 billion. A quarterly dividend of C$1.47 per common share was declared, payable on December 31.

What the company said about the market

Brindamour said that, at the industry level, these events reinforce firm market conditions. In insurance language, a firm market means prices are steady or rising and insurers are strict about terms. Insurance Business added its own commentary that catastrophe losses are keeping property pricing firm and that brokers should expect continued scrutiny of flood exposure, deductibles and mitigation documentation at renewal. That commentary is the publication's view, not a company forecast.

What it means for Canadian homeowners

Home insurance prices respond to claims. When floods, wind and wildfire push the property combined ratio above 100%, insurers usually seek rate increases, raise deductibles for water damage or ask for more detail on mitigation such as sump pumps and backwater valves. Homeowners can take practical steps: read the renewal notice for changes in deductibles and water coverage, ask the broker which flood and sewer backup options exist, and keep records of upgrades that reduce risk. The report does not say what rate changes Intact is seeking, so this article makes no estimate of price changes.

How to read a quarter like this

One quarter of heavy catastrophe losses does not by itself mean a company is in trouble. Intact's operating return on equity of 16% shows that investment income, distribution income and other lines absorbed the weather hit. It is the trailing total, now above guidance, that raises the question of whether pricing and reinsurance structures need to adjust. Insurers also buy reinsurance to cap their exposure, which is why the reported losses are described net of reinsurance.

What to watch next

Watch for Intact's fourth-quarter results, which will show whether weather losses stay elevated, and for rate filings in Ontario, Alberta and other provinces. Auto reform in Ontario and Alberta is also on the industry's agenda for 2027. The company publishes its quarterly reports and presentations on its investor relations website. This article summarises public reporting and is not financial advice.

A quarter of floods, wind and wildfire that pushed home insurance into an underwriting loss, while the company still earned a 16% operating return, shows why insurers keep pressing for firmer pricing and tighter terms on weather-exposed property.

title: Assurant Q3 Adjusted EPS Rises 7% to $6.15 and 2026 Outlook Goes Up
summary: Assurant reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $275.2 million, adjusted EBITDA up 8% to $464.4 million and adjusted EPS up 7% to $6.15, with Global Lifestyle earnings up 15%, and it raised its full-year outlook to about 10% growth in adjusted EBITDA excluding catastrophes.
description:
Assurant, a US insurer that specialises in protecting connected devices, vehicles and homes, reported its third-quarter 2026 results on November 3 and raised its outlook for the full year. Profit rose in both of its operating segments, and the company said growth was in double digits for the first nine months. This article summarises the figures in the company's earnings release as distributed by Business Wire, explains the main terms, and notes what the release does not say. It is a summary of public information and is not investment advice.

The headline numbers

For the third quarter of 2026, Assurant reported GAAP net income of $275.2 million, up 4% from $265.6 million in the third quarter of 2025. GAAP diluted earnings per share were $5.49, compared with $5.17, an increase of 6%. GAAP figures follow standard accounting rules and include items such as investment gains and losses.

The company also reports adjusted measures that strip out some of those items. Adjusted EBITDA, which is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation as the company defines it, rose 8% to $464.4 million from $431.5 million. Adjusted earnings per share rose 7% to $6.15 from $5.73. Excluding what Assurant calls reportable catastrophes, which are large weather events above a set threshold, adjusted EBITDA was $484.1 million, up 12% from $433.5 million, and adjusted EPS was $6.46, up 12% from $5.76. The gap between the two EBITDA figures, about $20 million, is our simple arithmetic and suggests catastrophe losses in the quarter were modest.

Global Lifestyle

Global Lifestyle is the larger of the two segments by revenue. It covers protection and support services for mobile devices and other connected products, vehicle protection and related services, usually sold through partners such as phone carriers, retailers and auto dealers. In the quarter it produced adjusted EBITDA of $236.9 million, up 15%, on net earned premiums, fees and other income of $2,661.1 million, up 11%.

The release does not break down which product lines drove the growth, and it does not give figures for individual partners, so readers cannot tell how much came from devices, vehicles or new programs. The 15% profit growth against 11% revenue growth shows that margins improved, since profit grew faster than sales.

Global Housing

Global Housing sells insurance related to homes, including lender-placed insurance, which is cover a mortgage servicer buys on a property when the owner's own policy lapses, along with renters insurance and related products. Its adjusted EBITDA was $268.3 million, up 5% from the third quarter of 2025. Excluding reportable catastrophes, it was $288.0 million, up 11%. Net earned premiums, fees and other income rose 6% to $744.9 million.

Together, the two segments produced net earned premiums, fees and other income of $3.41 billion, compared with $3.11 billion, an increase of 10%. The release does not give a single consolidated revenue figure, so that combined number covers the two operating segments only.

The raised outlook

Assurant raised its expectations for the full year. It now expects adjusted EBITDA excluding reportable catastrophes to grow about 10% from the 2025 base of $1,734 million, and adjusted EPS excluding reportable catastrophes to grow at a low double-digit rate from a base of $22.81. By segment, it expects Global Lifestyle adjusted EBITDA to grow at a mid-to-high teens rate, and Global Housing adjusted EBITDA excluding catastrophes to grow at a mid single-digit rate. It also expects the corporate and other segment to lose about $150 million of adjusted EBITDA.

Those percentages are ranges stated in words. The release does not give a dollar target for the full year, so any specific number would be an estimate. If growth of about 10% is applied to the base of $1,734 million, the implied figure is roughly $1.9 billion, but that calculation is ours and not company guidance.

Capital returned to shareholders

The company repurchased about 268 thousand shares for $75 million during the third quarter. In October it bought about 108 thousand more shares for $30 million. As of October 31, $469 million remained on its repurchase authorisation. Chief executive Keith Demmings said the company expects to return $350 million through share repurchases in 2026. A buyback reduces the number of shares outstanding, which can lift earnings per share even when total profit is unchanged, so investors often look at both measures together.

What it means for consumers

Most people meet Assurant without knowing it. A phone protection plan bought from a carrier, a service contract on a vehicle, or a renters policy might be provided behind the scenes by the company. Lender-placed insurance is different: it is charged to a homeowner whose own insurance has lapsed, usually at a higher cost than a normal policy, so keeping home insurance current is the best way to avoid it. Readers who are comparing protection plans can check what is covered, the deductible per claim, the number of claims allowed in a year, and who actually pays the claim, which is often a partner company rather than the retailer.

Reading the numbers with care

Adjusted figures help show underlying performance, but they are not a substitute for GAAP results, and a company decides which items to exclude. The gap between GAAP net income growth of 4% and adjusted EPS growth of 7% shows that some items outside the adjusted measure were less favorable in the quarter, although the release summary reviewed here does not itemise them. For a fuller picture, readers can compare the tables in the company's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

What to watch next

Watch Assurant's fourth-quarter results and its 2027 outlook, due after the year ends, the pace of buybacks against the $469 million remaining authorisation, and the weather season for housing losses. The company publishes its releases and presentations on its investor relations website. This article summarises public reporting and is not financial advice.

key_points: Assurant's third-quarter 2026 GAAP net income was $275.2 million, up 4% from $265.6 million, and GAAP diluted earnings per share were $5.49 against $5.17.
Adjusted EBITDA rose 8% to $464.4 million and adjusted EPS rose 7% to $6.15, and excluding reportable catastrophes the growth was 12% in both measures, to $484.1 million and $6.46.
Global Lifestyle, which covers device protection, auto and connected-living services, lifted adjusted EBITDA 15% to $236.9 million on revenue of $2.66 billion, up 11%.

Global Housing, the lender-placed and renters insurance business, earned $268.3 million of adjusted EBITDA, up 5%, or $288.0 million excluding catastrophes, up 11%, on revenue of $744.9 million, up 6%.

The company now expects about 10% growth in 2026 adjusted EBITDA excluding catastrophes and low double-digit growth in adjusted EPS on the same basis, and it plans about $350 million of share repurchases for the year.
why_it_matters: Assurant sells the protection behind many everyday purchases and mortgages, from phone insurance to cover that lenders place on a home when a borrower's policy lapses. Its results show how a specialty insurer can keep growing when household weather losses are mixed, and its updated outlook is a read on consumer spending on protection products.

title: Kemper Q3 Swings to $52.4M Profit as Premiums Fall 16%
summary: Kemper earned $52.4 million in the third quarter of 2026 against a $21.0 million loss a year earlier, as its specialty auto combined ratio improved to 99.2% from 104.8%, but about $23 million of favorable reserve development helped, earned premiums fell 16% to $857.9 million and book value per share fell 21% since year end after a $460 million goodwill charge.
description:
Kemper Corporation, a US insurer focused on non-standard auto insurance, reported full third-quarter 2026 results on November 9, after releasing preliminary figures on October 28. The quarter marked a return to profit after a large loss in the second quarter, but the improvement came with a smaller business and a helping hand from reserve releases. This article summarises the figures in the company's filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission and a report from Insurance Business, explains the main terms, and notes what is and is not known. It is a summary of public information, not investment advice.

The headline numbers

Kemper reported third-quarter net income attributable to the company of $52.4 million, or $0.88 per diluted share, compared with a net loss of $21.0 million, or $0.34 per share, in the same quarter of 2025. Adjusted consolidated net operating income, which removes certain items such as investment gains and impairments, was $59.9 million, or $1.01 per share, against $20.4 million, or $0.33 per share. In the second quarter of 2026, the company had reported a net loss of $464.8 million, driven by a $460.0 million non-cash goodwill impairment, which is an accounting charge that writes down the value of past acquisitions.

For the first nine months, the net loss is $414.1 million, or $7.04 a share, compared with net income of $151.3 million a year earlier, and adjusted net operating income is $98.7 million, compared with $210.9 million. So the third quarter's recovery has not yet made up for the weaker first half.

The specialty auto combined ratio

Kemper's Specialty Property and Casualty segment, which is mostly personal and commercial auto, reported a segment adjusted net operating income of $54.4 million, against $7.6 million. Its combined ratio, the percentage of premium that goes to claims and costs, was 99.2% compared with 104.8% a year earlier. A ratio below 100% means an underwriting profit, so the segment only just crossed into profitable territory.

Two details matter. First, the quarter included about $23 million of favorable prior-year reserve development, which means the company concluded that claims from earlier years would cost less than it had set aside. That lowered the combined ratio by 2.7 points, as Insurance Business pointed out in its headline that the improvement rests on those releases. Second, the underlying combined ratio, which excludes catastrophes and prior-year reserve changes, was 101.7%, compared with 99.6% a year earlier. The underlying figure shows that, before the reserve release, the current business still cost slightly more to run than it earned. Current-year catastrophe losses were small, at 0.2 points of the ratio.

A smaller book

Premiums fell sharply. Total specialty earned premiums were $857.9 million, down from $1,017.3 million, a decline of about 16%. Personal auto earned premiums dropped to $599.9 million from $785.1 million, while commercial auto rose to $258.0 million from $232.2 million. Net premiums written, the amount of business sold in the period, were $838.7 million against $982.2 million. The release does not split written premiums by line.

Shrinking while improving is a known approach in auto insurance. Companies that had underpriced risk raise rates, stop writing the least profitable business and accept losing customers. The report does not state how many policies were lost, and it says only that Kemper serves approximately 4.3 million policies in total, with no prior-year comparison. California, a large market for the company, shows the effect of rate action: the California personal auto combined ratio was 98.2%, compared with 110.6% in the first quarter of 2026, and the underlying ratio was 102.1% against 109.2% in that quarter. Insurance Business reported that regulators approved rate increases of 6.9% on two-thirds of the California book and 3% on the rest earlier this year.

Life insurance and investments

Kemper's life business is a steadier contributor. Life segment adjusted net operating income was $19.8 million, compared with $18.6 million, with earned premiums of $115.7 million against $99.8 million. Net investment income was $107.3 million, compared with $104.8 million.

Capital and the balance sheet

Book value per share, the accounting value of the company divided by its shares, was $36.20 at September 30, down 21% from $45.71 at the end of 2025, because of the goodwill write-down. Adjusted book value per share, which excludes some items, was $28.13, almost unchanged from $28.06. Total shareholders' equity was $2,133.3 million against $2,681.4 million. Long-term debt was $945.0 million, with $350.0 million of revolving credit capacity available, and the company paid a quarterly dividend of $0.32 per share on September 4.

What management said

Chief executive Stephen McAnena said the actions the company has taken to improve profitability are taking hold, and that there is more work ahead. Kemper will keep looking for efficiency opportunities through 2027 and expects to fully exit its Preferred Insurance business. The release gives no formal financial guidance for the year.

What it means for drivers

Drivers who buy non-standard auto insurance, which is aimed at people with prior accidents, lapses in coverage or lower credit scores, have felt the effect of these rate moves. When an insurer needs a better combined ratio, it usually raises premiums or declines applicants, so shopping around is useful. Ask each insurer what factors set the price, whether discounts are available for safe-driving programs, and whether the quote is for the full policy term. Some states also publish rate filings, so readers can check how much a company has been approved to raise prices.

What to watch next

Watch whether Kemper's underlying combined ratio moves below 100% without reserve releases, how quickly premiums stabilise after the decline, and the effect of exiting Preferred Insurance. The company's quarterly reports are on its investor relations site, and the full filing is available on the SEC's EDGAR system. This article summarises public reporting and is not financial advice.

title: IRDAI Orders Four-Layer Motor Policies From December 15
summary: IRDAI has told general insurers to sell private car and two-wheeler policies in four separate layers from December 15, 2026: compulsory third-party liability, optional liability for occupants or pillion riders, personal accident cover and own damage, with standard wording, an option form and a premium breakdown for each layer.
description:
India's insurance regulator has told general insurers to restructure motor insurance for private cars and two-wheelers into four clearly separated layers. The change, reported on November 4 and due to start on December 15, 2026, is meant to give buyers more choice and more transparency about what they are paying for. This article summarises what has been reported by Angel One and by the news agency IANS, explains each layer in plain language, and notes what has not been published. It is a summary of public reporting, not legal or financial advice, and readers should check the regulator's circular and their insurer's documents before making decisions.

What the regulator has ordered

According to the reports, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, known as IRDAI, directed general insurers to introduce a four-layer structure for motor insurance policies covering private cars and two-wheelers from December 15, 2026. Alongside the structure, insurers must use standardised policy wording for these vehicles, a uniform customer option form to record which covers the buyer chooses, and a Customer Information Sheet that lists each section of cover and its premium. Insurers must also complete integration with the Bima Sugam platform, the industry's online marketplace, so that the products are available there by the same date.

The reports say the regulator described the framework as aimed at improving customer choice and transparency by separating the components of a motor policy. They also say the circular was issued to comply with a Supreme Court order in the case of National Insurance Company Limited versus Thungala Dhana Laxmi and others. The sources reviewed do not explain the court's reasoning, so this article does not describe the case beyond its name.

The four layers

The first layer is third-party liability. It is compulsory under India's Motor Vehicles Act and covers the owner's legal liability for injury or death of another person, or damage to another person's property, caused by the insured vehicle. Without it, a vehicle cannot legally be driven on public roads.

The second layer is legal liability to occupants or pillion riders. It is optional. It covers passengers in a private car, pillion riders on a two-wheeler, and employees travelling in the insured vehicle, and the number of people covered cannot exceed the registered seating capacity. According to Angel One, it does not cover the owner-insured or immediate family, meaning parents, spouse and children.

The third layer is personal accident cover. Angel One reports that it is mandatory for the owner-insured, which fits the existing rule on compulsory personal accident cover for owner-drivers, and cover for other occupants, pillion riders or drivers other than the owner-driver can be bought separately. IANS describes the last three layers as optional, subject to the existing rules on compulsory personal accident cover. The reports differ slightly in wording, so readers should check the circular itself for the exact rule.

The fourth layer is own-damage cover, which pays for loss of or damage to the insured vehicle itself, such as after an accident, fire or theft depending on the policy terms. It is optional.

What changes for buyers

The most visible change is transparency. Each layer's premium must be shown separately, so a buyer can see how much the compulsory third-party part costs and how much each optional part adds. Until now, many buyers saw a single total. The new option form means the buyer's choices are recorded for every policy, and the Customer Information Sheet, available online and offline, must explain each component. The sources say the sheet must be provided at the time of sale.

Existing customers also get a new option. A person who holds a third-party-only policy can add liability cover for occupants or pillion riders during the policy term by paying an additional premium, without cancelling the existing policy. The sources do not say what that premium will be.

What does not change

Insurers will still be able to design new products and set the price of own-damage cover and additional covers, based on market conditions, even though the structure and wording are standardised. The reports do not say whether total premiums will rise or fall, and they give no figures, so any claim about price effects is unsupported. Competition between insurers, claims experience and the cost of repairs will continue to influence own-damage prices.

How to use the new structure

Buyers can prepare in a few practical ways. First, decide whether an own-damage layer is needed. For a new or financed vehicle, it is usually worth having, because it pays for the car or bike itself, while for an older vehicle some owners weigh the cost against the vehicle's value. Second, think about passengers. If the vehicle regularly carries family members, friends or colleagues, the occupant liability layer is a layer to ask about, keeping in mind that, according to the report, it excludes the owner and immediate family. Third, read the option form and the information sheet before signing, and keep copies. Fourth, ask the insurer how the premium for each layer is calculated, and compare quotes on a layer-by-layer basis, since standardised wording makes comparison easier.

What it means for insurers and agents

For insurers, the change means new documents, new systems and training for sales teams, with a deadline of December 15. Integration with Bima Sugam adds a further task. Agents and online platforms will need to explain the four layers clearly. Some may see lower revenue on optional covers if customers choose fewer layers, while others may see more interest in the add-on for passengers. The sources do not report industry reaction.

What to watch next

Watch for IRDAI's published circular, for insurers' updated policy wording and forms before December 15, for any clarification on the rule for owner personal accident cover, and for the first premium comparisons once the new structure is live. The regulator publishes its circulars on its website. This article summarises public reporting and is not legal or financial advice.
source_name: Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (motor circular reported November 4, 2026) as reported by Angel One and IANS
image_alt: Insurance and tax forms on a table beside a phone calculator and a pen (illustrative)
key_points: IRDAI has directed general insurers to offer motor policies for private cars and two-wheelers in a four-layer structure from December 15, 2026, with standardised policy wording across insurers.

The four layers are third-party liability, which stays compulsory, legal liability for occupants or pillion riders, personal accident cover and own-damage cover, and each layer's premium must be shown separately.
Insurers must collect a completed customer option form for each policy and give a Customer Information Sheet at the point of sale, online or offline, that explains each section and its premium.
Existing third-party policyholders can add occupant or pillion rider liability cover during the policy term by paying an additional premium, without cancelling the policy.

The reports say the circular follows a Supreme Court order in National Insurance Company versus Thungala Dhana Laxmi and others, and require insurers to complete integration with the Bima Sugam platform by the same date.
why_it_matters: Almost every vehicle owner in India buys motor insurance, and many do not know what each part of the premium pays for. Splitting a policy into clearly priced layers should make it easier to see what is compulsory, what is optional and what the buyer is actually paying for, and it changes how agents and websites have to explain the product.

title: Q3 2026 Insurer Scorecard: Who Made Money Underwriting
summary: A PolicyRix Team analysis ranks ten insurers by third-quarter 2026 combined ratio: reinsurers and specialty writers led with margins of 12 to 20 points, Canadian home insurers lost money underwriting on weather, and several car insurers improved their ratios by writing less business.
description:
Third-quarter results from ten property and casualty insurers and reinsurers were published in early November, and put side by side they tell a clearer story than any single report. This PolicyRix Team analysis ranks them by one measure, the combined ratio, adds what each company said about growth and catastrophe losses, and explains what the pattern suggests. All figures come from each company's own third-quarter 2026 results as covered in our earlier stories, and the calculations in this piece are ours. It is an analysis of public information and is not investment or insurance advice.

How to read the scorecard

The combined ratio adds claims and expenses and divides them by premium. Under 100% means the insurer made an underwriting profit, and over 100% means it paid out more than it earned from premiums. We turn each ratio into an underwriting margin by subtracting it from 100, so a combined ratio of 80% becomes a margin of 20 points. This is our own simple conversion for comparison, and it ignores investment income, which is large for insurers.

The ten are not identical businesses. Munich Re and Hannover Re are reinsurers, which insure other insurers. Palomar and Trisura are specialty writers. Mercury General, Safety Insurance, Root and Kemper are mostly car insurers. Intact and Definity are Canadian generalists with large home and auto books. Periods also differ: Hannover Re's figure covers nine months, the others cover the third quarter, and segments differ, so treat the ranking as a guide and not a verdict.

The ranking, best underwriting margin first

Munich Re's property and casualty reinsurance combined ratio was 80%, a margin of 20.0 points, even though it was 62.7% a year earlier. Palomar's was 80.8%, a margin of 19.2 points, and 76.3% on its adjusted basis. Hannover Re's nine-month property and casualty reinsurance ratio was 83.7%, a margin of 16.3 points. Trisura's was 87.5%, a margin of 12.5 points. Mercury General's was 90.2%, a margin of 9.8 points. Intact's group ratio was 94.0%, a margin of 6.0 points. Safety Insurance's was 96.3%, a margin of 3.7 points. Root's net combined ratio was 97.2%, a margin of 2.8 points. Kemper's specialty ratio was 99.2%, a margin of 0.8 points, and 101.7% before reserve releases, which is a negative margin of 1.7 points. Definity's was 100.6%, a negative margin of 0.6 points.

Pattern one: the reinsurers and specialty writers led

The top four are reinsurers and specialty companies. Munich Re's ratio rose sharply from a year earlier because major losses went from EUR 118 million to EUR 646 million, including EUR 300 million from the Colombian El Choco earthquake, yet the margin stayed the widest in the group. Major losses were 14.9% of net insurance revenue, below the 18% the company expected. Hannover Re's large losses of EUR 1,316 million for nine months were well under its budget of EUR 1,786.5 million. Palomar's catastrophe loss ratio was only 1.2%. In this quarter, the companies that carry risk for others, or that choose narrow niches, benefited from a light stretch for large losses, and that can change quickly.

Pattern two: Canadian home insurance took the weather hit

The two Canadian generalists were the weakest on weather. Intact reported about C$660 million of catastrophe losses, and its Canadian personal property combined ratio was 105.0%, with catastrophes adding 33 points. Definity's catastrophe losses were C$190.0 million and added 12.8 points to its group ratio, while its personal property ratio was 112.1% against 83.6% a year earlier, with catastrophes adding 32.6 points. Canadian home insurance in both books lost money on an underwriting basis in the quarter, while Definity's auto and commercial lines ran at about 96% and Intact's group ratio stayed under 100%. For a Canadian homeowner, this is the background to renewal notices that carry higher prices or larger deductibles.

Pattern three: some car insurers improved by shrinking

Four car-focused insurers show a different trade-off. Root's net combined ratio improved from 102.1% to 97.2%, but its gross written premium fell 8%, and the company said it chose to give up some direct-channel growth when expected returns fell below its threshold. Kemper's ratio improved from 104.8% to 99.2%, but specialty earned premium fell from $1,017.3 million to $857.9 million, and personal auto fell from $785.1 million to $599.9 million. Safety Insurance's ratio improved from 98.9% to 96.3%, with net written premiums down 4.2%. Mercury General went the other way, with net premiums earned up 9.6% and a ratio that worsened from 87.0% to 90.2%. The lesson is that a better ratio can come from writing less business, which raises margins now but does not by itself show lasting strength. For drivers, an insurer that is pulling back may offer fewer discounts or tighter acceptance rules.

Pattern four: headline profit and underwriting can disagree

Mercury General reported a net loss of $13.7 million because of realized investment losses of $261.9 million before tax, which the company linked mainly to higher market interest rates. Yet its operating income, which excludes those gains and losses, was $193.3 million, and its combined ratio was still a profit-making 90.2%. Kemper's quarter shows the reverse. It earned $52.4 million, but about $23 million of favorable reserve development, claims set aside in earlier years that turned out to be unneeded, took 2.7 points off its ratio. Headline net income and the underwriting result measure different things, and reading both avoids being misled by either.

What this analysis cannot tell us

One quarter is a snapshot. Catastrophe losses are lumpy, reinsurers report on different calendars, and the segments listed are not identical. We did not weight companies by size, and we did not include investment results, capital levels or guidance, which other measures capture. Readers who need a precise comparison should use the companies' own filings. The ratios here are as reported, and the margin and ranking are our calculations.

What to watch next

Watch fourth-quarter results, which include the heaviest weather and reinsurance renewal season, and rate filings from Canadian home insurers. The ten companies publish their results and presentations on their investor relations websites. This analysis was prepared by the PolicyRix Team from public reporting and is not financial advice.

Canadian home insurance took the weather hit: Intact's personal property combined ratio was 105.0% and Definity's was 112.1%, with catastrophes adding 33 and 32.6 points.
Root, Kemper and Safety improved their ratios while premiums fell 8%, 16% and 4.2%, which shows a better ratio can come from writing less business.

why_it_matters: A combined ratio shows whether an insurer makes money from insurance itself, before investment income. Comparing ten companies in the same quarter shows who benefited from light large losses, who was hit by weather, and who improved margins by shrinking, which helps readers judge renewal prices and company results beyond a single headline.
